description: We're a team of 6 students tackling the "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge. Our team has strong skills in data science, machine learning, and software development, plus cybersecurity expertise. We're building a decision-support tool that combines NASA Earth observation data with crop rotation strategies to help farmers adapt to climate change.
summary:
CULTIVA is a decision-support web platform that helps farmers in Morocco choose the right crop rotation: one that saves water, protects the soil and stays profitable. This matters because Morocco faces growing water stress and agriculture is the country’s largest water consumer, yet satellite data remains out of reach for most farmers.

CULTIVA turns NASA Earth observation data (SMAP soil moisture, GPM rainfall, NASA POWER climate, GRACE groundwater, MODIS vegetation, SRTM terrain, SoilGrids soil), combined with FAOSTAT yields, into clear recommendations. A farmer locates their plot, enters the previous crop and a priority, and CULTIVA proposes two rotations, each explained with water, soil, climate and yield scores, the agronomic rules applied and a sowing calendar. Falling groundwater (GRACE) and fragile vegetation (MODIS) make the engine stricter on water-hungry crops.

The interface is in French and Arabic with audio reading, and an Expert mode shows the full methodology. Our first version covers 13 zones in Fès-Meknès, and every result is labelled “favourable subject to validation”. We plan to extend CULTIVA to other regions of Morocco and beyond.
details:
CULTIVA is a web platform that recommends crop rotations to farmers in Morocco, based on NASA Earth observation data.

How it works: the farmer locates their plot by GPS, city name or map, and CULTIVA places it in one of 13 zones of the Fès-Meknès region (0.5° grid). The platform shows the state of the land (soil water, rainfall, groundwater, vegetation fragility, soil texture, slope) from NASA data. The farmer then chooses the soil type, the previous crop and a priority (save water, protect the soil, adapt to the climate, aim for yield, or balance). Our Python engine scores each of the 56 crops on four axes (water 0.30, soil 0.25, climate 0.15, yield 0.20), applies the agronomic rotation rules R01–R13 and proposes two rotations. Each one comes with its scores, the rules applied and a sowing calendar. GRACE groundwater trends and MODIS vegetation make the engine stricter where water is scarce.

Benefits: recommendations are explained, not a black box, so the farmer sees why a rotation is proposed. The interface is in French and Arabic with audio reading, and an Expert mode shows the full methodology.

Intended impact: help farmers save water, preserve the soil and stay profitable, starting in Fès-Meknès and extending to other regions of Morocco and beyond.

Tools: Python (pandas, numpy), FastAPI and Uvicorn for the backend; HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript with Three.js (3D globe) and MapLibre (map) for the frontend; NASA SMAP, GPM, POWER, GRACE/GRACE-FO, MODIS and SRTM data, plus SoilGrids and FAOSTAT; Git and GitHub. We used ChatGPT and Claude to help us code. No special hardware is needed.

Creativity: we combine several data sources, each with a precise role, into one transparent score, and we use groundwater and vegetation data as supervision layers. We recommend whole rotations rather than single crops.

Factors considered: honesty and limits. No figure is invented, missing data are excluded, and every proposal is labelled “favourable subject to validation”. The data are regional (0.5° grid), FAOSTAT yields are national, and 13 of the 56 crops have no yield data. The weights and rules are prototype choices to be validated with an agronomist. We also designed for accessibility: simple language, two languages and audio reading.
